lesson.title: The Voices That Demanded a Bill of Rights
lesson.summary: Anti-Federalists opposed ratifying the new Constitution in 1787 and 1788, warning that its strong national government threatened state sovereignty and individual liberty unless a bill of rights was added.
lesson.body:
When the Constitutional Convention finished its work in September 1787 and sent the new Constitution to the states for ratification, it did not receive automatic approval. A vocal and influential group of critics, who came to be called Anti-Federalists, argued that the convention had gone much too far, replacing a dangerously weak national government under the Articles of Confederation with one that swung too far in the opposite direction.

Prominent Anti-Federalists included Patrick Henry of Virginia, already famous for his fiery Revolutionary-era rhetoric, and George Mason, who had actually attended the Constitutional Convention as a Virginia delegate but refused to sign the finished document because it lacked, in his view, adequate protections for individual liberty. Mason had earlier authored the Virginia Declaration of Rights in 1776, and he wanted something similar built into the new national framework. Richard Henry Lee wrote influential letters under the pen name the Federal Farmer, while writers using the name Brutus, likely New York judge Robert Yates, published essays warning that the new government would inevitably grow to swallow up the states.

Anti-Federalist objections centered on a handful of recurring fears. They worried the Constitution created a national government too far removed from ordinary citizens to be held accountable, with a House of Representatives so small relative to the growing population that few Americans would ever really know their representative. They feared the necessary and proper clause, which allowed Congress to pass laws needed to carry out its other powers, gave the national government dangerously open-ended authority to expand its own reach over time. And they were alarmed that the document, as originally drafted, contained no bill of rights at all, leaving basic protections like freedom of speech, freedom of religion, and protection from unreasonable searches entirely unmentioned.

That last objection proved the most politically potent. In state after state, ratifying conventions saw Anti-Federalist delegates demand assurances that a bill of rights would be added once the Constitution took effect, and Federalist supporters, recognizing they needed Anti-Federalist votes to secure ratification in closely divided states like Massachusetts and Virginia, increasingly agreed to that bargain rather than risk defeat.

The Constitution was ultimately ratified without Anti-Federalists getting everything they wanted, but their pressure directly produced the first ten amendments that would follow soon after. In that sense the Anti-Federalists lost the immediate fight over ratification but shaped the Constitution's final form nearly as much as its original framers did, a legacy that the Federalist Papers, written to answer exactly these objections, help illuminate.
